question: Is the reversal curse intrinsic to autoregressive transformers, or does it arise when surface names fail to bind to consistent, disentangled concepts?

key_findings.claim: Standard decoder-only transformers can infer reversal when entities and relations are represented directly as concept embeddings.
key_findings.evidence: On synthetic one-to-one relations, models of one to eighteen layers reach MRR from 0.81 to 0.98 as the concept-level induction set grows, without reverse-data augmentation or a non-causal loss.

key_findings.claim: The same models fail at surface-level names, and controlled name overlap and depth support the authors' consistency-and-entanglement hypothesis.
key_findings.evidence: Surface-language modeling yields 0% reversal accuracy across architecture variants. JEPA concept prediction recovers non-trivial transfer, but accuracy falls with recognition/semantic depth and with name-token multiplicity.

key_findings.claim: Sparse memory layers improve reversal beyond simply widening the transformer, but only after concept-level prediction addresses representational inconsistency.
key_findings.evidence: At similar effective parameter counts, a wide top-k memory recognition layer produces a large generalization gain; attaching memory layers to ordinary surface-level language modeling still fails.

key_findings.claim: The learned reversible parametric memory outperforms tested frontier models using long non-parametric contexts on synthetic forward chaining.
key_findings.evidence: For three-hop arithmetic trees averaging 0.4K to 6.5K facts, JEPA plus memory degrades mildly as branching grows, while o3-mini and Gemini-2.5-Pro degrade more; precise plotted values are not tabulated.

method.core_idea: Separate surface-name recognition from semantic processing, predict the target in a concept embedding space with an in-batch contrastive JEPA loss, and optionally use a sparse memory layer for disentangled recognition.
method.mechanism: Concept-level prediction forces subject and object occurrences toward a shared representation; top-k memory activations reduce gradient interference between distinct surface names, enabling inverse association and parametric forward chaining.
assumptions: The experimenter knows where concept representations should be read and predicted.
Each synthetic name maps to one unique concept.
Synthetic reversible one-to-one relations reflect an important component of real factual binding.

techniques.role: Moves autoregressive supervision from surface tokens to learned entity representations.
Discriminates the correct target concept from other active concepts.
Reduces cross-concept gradient interference from overlapping names.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic reversal over direct concept embeddings
evaluations.result: MRR reaches 0.975 in one reported large-data configuration.
evaluations.baseline: Standard transformers at other depths and induction-set sizes

evaluations.setting: Two-token surface names with controlled multiplicity
evaluations.result: Standard LM is 0%; JEPA is non-trivial and worsens with depth/overlap; memory layers improve it.
evaluations.baseline: Surface-level LM, wider transformer, and JEPA without memory

evaluations.setting: Three-hop arithmetic trees with up to 6.5K facts
evaluations.result: Parametric JEPA-memory models show the strongest plotted scaling.
evaluations.baseline: Standard transformer, o3-mini, and Gemini-2.5-Pro with facts in context

limitations: The proposed solution requires known concept locations and task-specific scaffolding.
Unique synthetic names omit synonymy, polysemy, open-world concept acquisition, and noisy language.
The binding and entanglement mechanisms are supported by interventions but are not uniquely identified causal explanations.
failure_modes: Deeper recognition and semantic stacks accumulate interference.
Higher surface-token multiplicity collapses reversal accuracy.
A one-name-one-memory-slot design impedes synonymy and dynamic concept formation.
reusable_insights: Test an architectural impossibility at the latent concept level before attributing a surface-level failure to the core sequence model.
Representation consistency and interference are separable axes for memory design.
Reversal can be evaluated as an enabling primitive for multi-step parametric inference, not only inverse recall.
open_questions: Can concept slots be discovered without supervision in realistic corpora?
Do the interventions improve natural-entity reversal without sacrificing ordinary language modeling?
Can causal tracing distinguish consistency repair from easier contrastive retrieval?

competitive_landscape.title: The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on A is B fail to learn B is A
competitive_landscape.difference: Berglund et al. establish the failure in factual learning; this work proposes a concept-binding mechanism and targeted architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.2, Knowledge Manipulation
competitive_landscape.difference: Allen-Zhu and Li document near-zero inverse knowledge search despite storage; this paper separates direct-concept success from surface-name failure and intervenes on recognition.

competitive_landscape.title: Large Concept Models: Language Modeling in a Sentence Representation Space
competitive_landscape.difference: Large Concept Models autoregress over sentence representations at broad scale; the present JEPA predicts entity concepts inside a controlled factual-binding task.

novelty_assessment: Reviewer inference: reversal failures, non-causal fixes, JEPA, and sparse memory layers all predate the paper. The new contribution is the controlled concept-versus-surface decomposition and the combination of concept prediction with sparse recognition to overcome reversal without adding reversed facts.
reviewer_notes: Full main text and appendices were checked. The binding account remains a mechanistic hypothesis, and the frontier-model comparison mixes parametric training with long-context inference. Primary records checked 2026-08-23.
